title: Watchfulness, again
hook: knowing He sees you, recalled from earlier in the path

segments.voice: Yesterday, tawbah, the first station, and your line: turn back. Did you make the amends you chose? Today, the station that keeps a turned person facing the right way. Day one thousand two hundred seventy-one.

A boy is minding a flock of sheep in the hills. A traveler comes by, the companion Abdullah ibn Umar, so the story goes, and tests him. Sell me one sheep, he says. Tell your master a wolf took it. Who would know? The boy looks at him and answers with a question: then where is Allah? It's a story people tell, found in later collections rather than the major hadith books. But the boy's answer holds today's whole lesson.
screen: `A SHEPHERD BOY IN THE HILLS.` → `WHO WOULD KNOW?` → `THEN WHERE IS ALLAH?`

segments.voice: The word is muraqabah, watchfulness: living with the awareness that Allah sees you. We met the idea much earlier in the path, with ihsan. In the hadith of Jibril, in Sahih al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim, the angel asks the Prophet, peace be upon him, what ihsan is. The answer: to worship Allah as though you see Him, and if you don't see Him, He sees you. That second half is muraqabah. You may not feel the presence. The watching doesn't depend on your feeling it. The Qur'an says it plainly. In Pickthall's translation: "Lo! Allah hath been a Watcher over you." And elsewhere, that He is with you wherever you are. Now, why come back to it here, after repentance? Because in the books of the inward path, the stations lean on each other. Tawbah turns you around. Muraqabah keeps you turned. A person who has just made amends can drift right back, unless something holds their attention. Watchfulness is that something. Here's a detail worth noticing. In the shepherd story, the boy isn't afraid of being caught. Nobody is there to catch him. What stops him is simpler: he knows he's seen. That's the difference between watchfulness and anxiety. It isn't a security camera that makes you nervous. It's closer to the way you speak differently when someone you love is in the room. The teachers of the path describe it as a steady awareness of the heart, in prayer and outside it. In an ordinary day it shows up in small places: the receipt you could fudge, the comment you could post anonymously, the shortcut nobody would notice. He sees.
screen: `MURAQABAH: AWARE THAT HE SEES.` · `IHSAN: IF YOU DON'T SEE HIM, HE SEES YOU.` · `TAWBAH TURNS; WATCHFULNESS KEEPS.` · then, large: `NOT A CAMERA: A PRESENCE.`

segments.voice: The practice: sit, aware of being seen. Settle, and breathe. Let your shoulders drop. Now, without forcing anything, hold this one thought: I am seen, right now, as I am. Not judged, not graded. Seen. Notice what happens in your body. Maybe your posture shifts. Maybe something softens. If your mind wanders, that's fine; come back to the thought. If you pray, you can rest in the line from the hadith: if you don't see Him, He sees you. If not, simply rest in being seen. The bell holds the time.
Muraqabah. Watchfulness: living with the awareness that Allah sees you, the second half of ihsan. Today's word.
Your line: he sees. Today, at one moment when nobody would know, act as you would if somebody did. Tomorrow, accounting for yourself. Day one thousand two hundred seventy-one.

howItsDone: In the Islamic inward path, muraqabah is the cultivated awareness that Allah sees, drawn from the hadith of Jibril; some Sufi orders also use the word for a practice of quiet, attentive sitting.
